title_en: Apple Wallet vs. Google Wallet: What are the differences between them?
title_fa: Apple Wallet vs. Google Wallet: What are the differences between them?
excerpt_en: Whether you use Apple Pay or Google Pay mostly depends on your device, but there are some small ways they differ that you might not notice at first.
excerpt_fa: Whether you use Apple Pay or Google Pay mostly depends on your device, but there are some small ways they differ that you might not notice at first.
content_en:
Apple Wallet vs. Google Wallet: What are the differences between them?
Both serve the same purposes, but there are some subtle differences.
Apple Wallet and Google Wallet, as their names suggest, have similar purposes. You use them as your digital wallet: a secure place to keep your payment cards, tickets and other everyday passes on your phone. Apple Pay and Google Pay are the services that handle the payments, but it's the Wallet apps that store everything. The names are often used interchangeably, though they refer to different parts of a connected process.
As long as the retailer accepts mobile payments and your card's payment network, and your card provider supports the wallet service, you should be able to use your digital cards to pay in-store and online. Which one you use is dictated by whether you own an iPhone or an Android phone. They're both similar in the basics, but have some differences in what you can add and how you're able to use them.
Both tools offer similar core functionality
Google and Apple both want the Wallet app to be your go-to place for everything you'd otherwise stick in your physical wallet or purse. Credit and debit cards are the obvious items, but this also also includes loyalty cards, gift cards, boarding passes, event tickets, and train or bus tickets. It can even hold NFC-supported passes, like a digital hotel key or car key, as well as workplace access cards for buildings. This all depends on your location and whether the company providing the pass supports digital wallets. As long as NFC support is there, there's a chance it'll work.
Getting your payment cards into either app is straightforward. In Apple Wallet, tap the plus button and choose Debit or Credit Card. In Google Wallet, tap Add to Wallet > Payment card. You'll need to follow the prompts, then verify with your bank or card provider. As long as the issuing entity supports this function, the card should then be set up for you to use.
Some differences become apparent in support for other passes. Apple Wallet expects items you're adding to officially support digital wallets; you'll usually see an Add to Apple Wallet button in emails, apps or similar. This is useful, as it means the Wallet app can support specific features. For instance, if an airline supports it, a boarding pass will automatically update with gate numbers, while also showing up on your Apple Watch. The experience is uniform, with a strict Apple template for passes and cards. Though in iOS 27, you can now add custom passes for otherwise unsupported items.
Google Wallet has been more flexible for a longer time. It offers official Add to Google Wallet passes and can also import tickets and boarding passes from your Gmail inbox. More importantly, though, is its Everything Else option for digitizing photos of random cards and passes in your wallet. This makes it easy to store a parking, library or gym card. They'll lack the live updates, but this support means you can move to a fully digital setup, even for the analog items in your wallet.
Apple Wallet keeps you going when your battery dies
Both Google Wallet and Apple Wallet are supposed to offer seamless experiences, which they do for the most part. Google Wallet is accessible through a web interface, while Apple Wallet isn't.
To pay in-person using an iPhone with Face ID, you'll normally double-click the side button, authenticate with your face or passcode, then hold your phone near the reader. Older iPhones use Touch ID instead. With Google Wallet, you don't need to press a button; just unlock your phone and hold it near the contactless reader. Your default card will handle the payment; you'll need to open the app to choose another card. With Apple Wallet, you can pick a card before paying.
You can customize this slightly. If your iPhone has the Action button, you can assign a Shortcut to open Wallet, although this isn't terribly useful since double-pressing the Side button already does this. Google Wallet supports shortcuts too, including a double-press of the power button on certain Pixel phones. This is worth using if you often pay with different cards.
You can also pay from your wrist with an Apple Watch or a compatible NFC-enabled Wear OS watch. Double-click the side button on Apple Watch or open Google Wallet on Wear OS, then hold your watch near the reader to make the payment.
Both apps can quickly make transit payments without authentication when you hop onto a supported bus, train or tram. Apple Wallet's Express Mode lets you use eligible cards without waking or unlocking your iPhone, while Google Wallet's Express Pay will also make transit payments without verification (though your phone screen needs to be on). Apple's got the advantage here: on supported iPhones, eligible Express Cards can work for up to five hours after the battery runs out. This doesn't work if you turn off the phone yourself.
Digital ID support depends on where you live
Digital IDs are a little more complicated. Unlike the banking world, support for digital IDs rests on states and governments. Thus, where you live matters more than anything, and advancements can take a long time.
Google Wallet can create an ID pass from a passport issued by certain countries, but it isn't a replacement for the physical document and won't be universally accepted. Apple lets you add a driver's license or state ID from participating US states and territories, but you'll still need your physical ID wherever the digital version isn't accepted (a lot of places, currently). Google Wallet also supports digital IDs, but like Apple Wallet, the support varies.
Even if your government has a digital ID program, there's no guarantee that it'll include support for Google Wallet or Apple Wallet. For instance, in the UK, plans for a digital driver's license that acts as a form of ID and is intended as an alternative to photographic ID cards are still progressing. However, the British government has said these will be exclusively...

title_en: Waymo's robotaxis are now available in Las Vegas
title_fa: Waymo's robotaxis are now available in Las Vegas
excerpt_en: Waymo's fully autonomous rides will initially serve those around the city's main strip.
excerpt_fa: Waymo's fully autonomous rides will initially serve those around the city's main strip.
content_en:
Waymo's robotaxis are now available in Las Vegas
The fully autonomous rides will initially serve those around the city’s main strip.
Waymo and its fleet of robotaxis has made its way into Nevada, starting with Las Vegas. The company announced its expansion would be limited to a 24-mile service area surrounding the Las Vegas Strip, but would later widen the service footprint to cover more of the surrounding Clark County.
According to Waymo, the robotaxi fleet on Vegas roads will mostly be the Ojai all-electric minivans that are equipped with the sixth-generation Waymo Driver hardware meant to handle harsh weather conditions.
Last month, the Nevada Transportation Authority approved Waymo's application for an Autonomous Vehicle Network Company permit, leading up to its service launch in Clark County, which includes Las Vegas. The state authority also granted Tesla and Uber the same approvals, meaning those visiting should expect to see more driverless cars going up and down the strip. However, Zoox was the first robotaxi service to launch in Vegas, dating back to September of last year, and later expanded its footprint in Sin City.
Prior to expanding to Las Vegas, Waymo announced the launch of its robotaxi service in Denver, San Diego and Tampa, Florida earlier this month. However, the Alphabet subsidiary has grown its coverage beyond the US, even launching its robotaxi fleet in Munich, Germany in August.

title_en: Elon Musk's X Corp and SpaceXAI just moved to dismiss their lawsuit against Apple
title_fa: Elon Musk's X Corp and SpaceXAI just moved to dismiss their lawsuit against Apple
excerpt_en: A lawsuit from last year accused the iPhone-maker of suppressing apps like Grok on the App Store.
excerpt_fa: A lawsuit from last year accused the iPhone-maker of suppressing apps like Grok on the App Store.
content_en:
Elon Musk's X Corp and SpaceXAI just moved to dismiss their lawsuit against Apple
The original complaint accused the iPhone-maker of suppressing apps like Grok on the App Store.
Elon Musk's X Corp and SpaceXAI have moved to dismiss a lawsuit against Apple, according to a court filing. The suit has been resolved in a federal court in Texas, though we don't have any details as to the reasoning behind the dismissal.
We also don't know if some kind of settlement has been reached. Engadget has reached out to Apple for more information. We'll update this post when we hear back.
The original lawsuit was brought forth by Musk's companies last year and accused Apple of violating antitrust laws. This was because the company integrated ChatGPT tools into Apple Intelligence, which "locked up markets to maintain their monopolies and prevent innovators like X and xAI from competing."
The complaint also suggested that both Apple and OpenAI were conspiring against SpaceXAI's products, like the occasionally Adolph Hitler-praising chatbot Grok. It went on to accuse Apple of not promoting its apps on the App Store.
"If not for its exclusive deal with OpenAI, Apple would have no reason to refrain from more prominently featuring the X app and the Grok app in its App Store," the company once told Reuters.
It's worth noting that many of OpenAI's rivals had apps that spent some time at the top of the App Store charts, even after the partnership with Apple. This includes both DeepSeek and Perplexity, though not SpaceXAI.
OpenAI was also named in the original lawsuit. Musk's companies say it will continue to pursue claims against the ChatGPT maker, according to a report by CNBC. Today's dismissal only pertains to Apple.
xAI's decision to create and host a breeding ground for predators to spread nonconsensual sexually explicit AI deepfakes, including images that digitally undress children, is vile.
I am calling on the Attorney General to immediately investigate the company and hold xAI...
— Governor Gavin Newsom (@CAgovernor) January 14, 2026
SpaceXAI is currently embroiled in another lawsuit. This one involves accusations that Grok was used to generate thousands of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) images. There are also allegations that it facilitates "the large-scale production of deepfake nonconsensual intimate images that are being used to harass women and girls across the internet." This led to an official investigation by authorities in California, which is ongoing.
Whoever could guess why the Grok app to the top of those App Store charts? It's just gotta be market manipulation.

title_en: Volkswagen’s crazy-efficient EV borrows an idea from Slate
title_fa: Volkswagen’s crazy-efficient EV borrows an idea from Slate
excerpt_en: Volkswagen's new efficiency-minded halo car is almost twice as efficient as the most efficient production car, the Lucid Air.
excerpt_fa: Volkswagen's new efficiency-minded halo car is almost twice as efficient as the most efficient production car, the Lucid Air.
content_en:
Volkswagen took the covers off a new prototype electric vehicle Monday, one that’s capable of hitting the equivalent of 323 miles per gallon under ideal conditions, making it one of the most efficient cars in the world.
It’s not unusual for automakers to float pie-in-the-sky concepts with outlandish stats, but Volkswagen took it a step or two further by building the EV and driving it from its home base in Wolfsburg, Germany, on a 794-mile (1,278-kilometer) trip to Vienna. The team charged the Mission Efficiency prototype once during the journey and arrived with 104 miles (168 kilometers) of range left, resulting in consumption of 7.51 kilowatt-hours per 100 miles, or about 279 MPGe.
The teardrop-shaped Mission Efficiency prototype was built using the electric motor and battery from the ID. Polo, two features that bring the car to “near production” status, Volkswagen said in a press release.
For those keeping score, the prototype is almost twice as efficient as the most efficient production car in the world, the Lucid Air Pure.
By some back-of-the-envelope math, Volkswagen’s science experiment can get more than 400 miles of range out of a 54.9-kilowatt-hour battery, though that’s not an official EPA rating. Lucid gets 420 miles from an 84-kilowatt-hour battery per EPA ratings, but it’s a much larger and more practical vehicle.
Volkswagen had to make some compromises in the name of efficiency.
The most noticeable is the roofline, which tapers quickly after peaking above the driver’s head. The shape, known as a Kammback, is among the most aerodynamic shapes a vehicle can take. Volkswagen was able to bring the coefficient of drag down to 0.158, while also keeping the frontal area low at just 2.08 square meters.
As a result, the Mission Efficiency is technically a 2+2, meaning the rear seats aren’t suitable for most adults. Volkswagen said the backseat is designed for people shorter than 5-foot 3 inches, or about 1.6 meters.
“The prototype was designed so that it could theoretically be used by a young family of four,” Volkswagen said, though anyone who has contemplated sitting in a 2+2 knows that even kids might scoff at the notion.
Another compromise sits closer to the road. Because wheels and tires can contribute about a quarter to a third of aerodynamic drag, the designers tightened the space between the wheel arches and the front tires. It’s great for efficiency, but probably not great for ride quality since wheels need space to move inside the wheel wells so the shocks can absorb bumps.
One place Volkswagen didn’t compromise was the mirrors. Sideview mirrors generate a lot of drag just by hanging off the sides, and while cameras would have cut into those losses significantly, they don’t offer the same sense of depth that true mirrors do.
To top it all off, Volkswagen put solar cells on the roof and the trunk lid. It’s a nice touch that’s sure to delight the internet, but their impact is limited, adding just 18 miles (30 kilometers) to perfectly flat, sunny routes driven at a constant 42.25 mph (68 kph).
Inside, the seats are built using lightweight materials and designs. On the dash, Volkswagen took a page from EV startup Slate Auto. Like Slate’s bare-bones pickup, the Mission Efficiency doesn’t come with an infotainment system or built-in speakers. Instead, it offers a portable Bluetooth speaker and assumes drivers will bring their own devices.
While Volkswagen frequently calls the Mission Efficiency a “near production” vehicle, the company didn’t commit to actual production. Though don’t assume it won’t: Over a decade ago, the automaker produced 250 examples of the XL1, another efficiency-minded halo car. And like other halo cars, it didn’t come cheap, with prices starting at €110,000 in 2013.

title_en: Netflix is making movies based on Crazy Taxi and Stranger than Heaven
title_fa: Netflix is making movies based on Crazy Taxi and Stranger than Heaven
excerpt_en: Netflix's deal with Sega includes a new Sonic animated series as well as movies based on Crazy Taxi and Stranger than Heaven.
excerpt_fa: Netflix's deal with Sega includes a new Sonic animated series as well as movies based on Crazy Taxi and Stranger than Heaven.
content_en:
Netflix is making movies based on Crazy Taxi and Stranger than Heaven
A new Sonic animated series is also in development as part of a deal with Sega.
Netflix and Sega are teaming up for more movie and TV adaptations of video games. The first project that's bubbling away is a film based on a series that's well known for its gripping narrative, Crazy Taxi. Dan Gregor and Doug Mand, the writers of last year's enjoyable reboot of The Naked Gun, are writing the script.
The movie — which appears to be a live-action comedy — will likely arrive after the next game in the series, Crazy Taxi World Tour. That's set to arrive next year.
Also on deck is a live-action crime film based on Stranger Than Heaven, the next title from Yakuza/Like A Dragon developer RGG Studio. That action-adventure game will hit PC and consoles on January 15.
In addition, Netflix will be the home of another Sonic animated series, following Sonic Prime. The upcoming show will be made with pre-schoolers in mind. Netflix said in a press release it'll be "a high-voltage, comedic, yet emotionally grounded series built for kids who want to feel a little edge, a little attitude and a lot of 'that's my crew' wish fulfillment."
Netflix has a boatload of other game adaptations in the works, including a live-action Assassin's Creed series set in ancient Rome and a reality cooking competition show based on Overcooked. During BlizzCon over the weekend, Blizzard revealed an animated series based on Diablo is coming to Netflix while hinting that adaptations of other franchises are in the works. Before all of those, a second season of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners will land on Netflix next month.

title_fa: TIFF 2026: The latest movie reviews from Toronto

content_en:
If you want an idea of what’s next in film, the Toronto International Film Festival is a good place to start. Every year TIFF features a huge range of features from around the world, and often some of them go on to be huge hits or awards contenders; the 2025 edition, for instance, included the likes of both Hamnet and Obsession.
Covering a sprawling festival like TIFF solo is next to impossible, so I do my best to see as much as I can, and then write about everything with bite-sized reviews published each day. For 2026, that means exciting upcoming films like Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, and a gigantic Elon Musk documentary, and even a few streaming series, like Crystal Lake and Carrie.
You can keep up with my thoughts on everything I watch right here.
The four-hour-long Elon Musk documentary might be preaching to the choir
It makes sense that Musk is a long film. The latest from Alex Gibney, who has previously directed documentaries about Theranos and Steve Jobs, is an impressively thorough retelling of the story of Elon Musk, from his early days as a dot-com millionaire to “taking a wood chipper” to vital US government departments. In order to understand Musk’s rise to power, you need to know the whole story. Musk tells it compellingly and convincingly, but doesn’t offer much in the way of revelations if you’re aware of Musk’s catastrophic influence on the world. For everyone else, a demanding runtime just shy of four hours might prove too much of a barrier to being convinced.
The film opens with shots of space and a voiceover of Musk detailing some of his sci-fi ambitions. From there, it’s a fairly chronological narrative of how we got to this point. The first section of the film reveals how Musk’s mythology was built, while also steadily seeding doubts that he’s the Tony Stark–style tycoon that many believe him to be. It starts off with the basic details, like when Musk was ousted as CEO from PayPal or how he convinced the world he founded Tesla, a company that existed before he was involved. The film juxtaposes his many bombastic claims about autonomous vehicles with visceral footage of a deadly crash involving a Tesla on autopilot. It drops in poignant interviews, like when former MAGA influencer Ashley St Clair, mother to one of Musk’s many children, declares in a terrified voice: “Elon is a nuke.”
Read Article >Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother will make you forget all about Marvel’s Blade disaster
Marvel’s mishandling of its Blade reboot will likely go down as one of the studio’s biggest mistakes. There was a great actor in place to play the vampire hunter (Mahershala Ali), and a promising director set to take over the reins (Bassam Tariq). In retrospect, though, the disappointing demise of Blade might not be such a bad thing, because Tariq and Ali have collaborated on something much more interesting than a superhero reboot: the powerful hitman thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.
That was one of five movies I was able to cram into a very hectic third day at the Toronto International Film Festival (you can see my previous reports here and here), and it was one of those days that drives home why events like TIFF can be so special. Each film I saw was drastically different from the last — there was everything from a drama about drifting cars to a throwback horror flick based on a famous Japanese ghost story — which was a great reminder that there are still plenty of new ideas left in the world of film.

Due to a scheduling mishap, I was only able to check out two movies on my second day at the Toronto International Film Festival — but I did manage to get an early look at and some fascinating details on one of my most anticipated films this year.
Even if you don’t know the name Laika, you probably know the studio’s work; it’s the animation house behind stop-motion hits like ParaNorman, The Boxtrolls, and Kubo and the Two Strings. Over the years Laika’s films have steadily gotten more impressive on both a technical and artistic level. Which brings us to the incredible-looking Wildwood, hitting theaters next month. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s a look:

Hello once again from Toronto, where for a week every year I watch far too many movies and tell you all about them. The festival, better known as TIFF, is always a great preview of the months ahead in film, with a nice mix of mainstream fare, awards contenders, indie surprises, and genre flicks destined to be cult classics. The streamers also love to make their presence felt here, previewing some of their most anticipated projects. Last year, for instance, Netflix showed off both Guillermo del Toro’s long-awaited Frankenstein as well as the third Knives Out movie, and I was also able to watch everything from the terrifying video game adaptation Exit 8 to Park-Chan wook’s dark satire No Other Choice.
This year looks similarly promising. There are new films from directors like Takashi Miike, Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, and Werner Herzog, and very intriguing features including a four-hour-long documentary on Elon Musk. There are also previews of a surprising number of Halloween-adjacent streaming series in the form of Netflix’s Below, Peacock’s Crystal Lake, and Amazon’s Carrie. I’m aiming to see just shy of 30 films and series over the next week or so, and, just like last year, I’ll be writing daily dispatches covering every single thing I see with a brief review.

title_en: How to know if your USB-C ports can support video
title_fa: How to know if your USB-C ports can support video
excerpt_en: Your USB-C port can do a lot, but it won't necessarily be able to transfer video. Understanding what yours can do makes it easy to choose the best video option.
excerpt_fa: Your USB-C port can do a lot, but it won't necessarily be able to transfer video. Understanding what yours can do makes it easy to choose the best video option.
content_en:
How to know if your USB-C ports can support video
Not all USB-C ports are created equal. Don’t find out the hard way.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Since its introduction in 2014, USB-C has become the primary connection method for laptops, phones, tablets, game controllers and other devices. For the most part, this provides a much simpler experience since you aren't required to collect an endless set of cables for various device. But it's still not perfect, with the crux of the problem being that not all USB-C ports and cables are created equal despite their shared standard.
While some USB-C connections are able to carry a video signal, others are only capable of charging your device. Ideally, everything would have do-it-all USB-C connections for handling data transfer, charging and audiovisual output. But this isn't realistic.
Thus, the secret to solving your USB-C port conundrum is hidden in each product's specifications. But what should you look for to know if your devices and cables support video output?
Understanding DisplayPort Alternate Mode
The best way to know if your USB-C setup supports video transfer is checking whether it supports DisplayPort Alternate Mode. Built into many USB-C accessories, DP Alt Mode allows your USB-C cable to carry video signals using the DisplayPort protocol. This is a digital display interface (which you might be familiar with from desktop PCs and monitors) that supports high resolutions and speedy refresh rates. DP Alt Mode enables a single cable to transfer both data and audiovisual displays. Critically, DP Alt Mode connections require that all three parts (the device, display and cable joining the two) are DP Alt Mode compatible.
Unfortunately, many of the older iterations of USB standards do not support DP Alt Mode. USB 3.1 and 3.2 devices may support it, but this is dependent on the manufacturer. However, newer connection standards mandate baked-in support for DP Alt Mode, such as USB4 supporting both power transfer and video.
All generations of Thunderbolt connections that use USB-C (Thunderbolt 3 through 5), marked by the familiar lightning icon, offer high-speed data and video transfers including DP Alt Mode. Thunderbolt 3 offers similar capabilities as USB4, while Thunderbolt 4 and 5 provide several performance upgrades. Although they're more expensive than their Thunderbolt 3 counterparts, opting for the latest versions of the standard can enhance your experience by powering multiple monitors with better refresh rates and higher resolutions.
Knowing whether your devices are DP Alt Mode compatible can be difficult. Some manufacturers put the port type on the device, such as the lighting symbol next to Thunderbolt ports. Other may add a DP icon beside a USB-C port to demonstrate its DP Alt Mode capabilities. If you don't see any clues on the devices or cables, check the manual or search for product specs online to confirm support for DisplayPort Alternate Mode.
What to do if your USB-C port doesn't support video
If you discover that a USB-C port or cable doesn't support video, there are workarounds. If your device has an HDMI port, you can use an HDMI cable compatible with both your device and display to deliver video output. For the most part, modern HDMI cables support up to 8K visuals and high dynamic range, meaning you're likely to get comparative visual results as you would through a USB-C port. However, not all HDMI ports and cables are created equal. To get the highest resolutions and refresh rates, opt for at least HDMI 2.0, with HDMI 2.1 or later being best for modern setups.
If your display doesn't have HDMI input, you can try an active adapter like the StarTech USB-A 3.0 to Dual HDMI Adapter. These let you run HDMI output from a USB port that's not normally capable of doing so. Because these rely on internal software and bandwidth, they introduce overhead and thus aren't ideal for gamers or anyone who wants super-high resolutions or refresh rates. Normal adapters, like USB-C hubs that have an HDMI port or USB-C to HDMI cables, won't work if your laptop doesn't support DP Alt Mode.
Otherwise, wireless display options like AirPlay or Miracast are a backup for casting your display to a TV or monitor without cables.

title_en: Siri AI is here as Apple releases iOS 27, macOS Golden Gate and other major OS updates
title_fa: Siri AI is here as Apple releases iOS 27, macOS Golden Gate and other major OS updates
excerpt_en: The kinks are still being worked out for users in the EU and China though.
excerpt_fa: The kinks are still being worked out for users in the EU and China though.
content_en:
Siri AI is here as Apple releases iOS 27, macOS Golden Gate and other major OS updates
The public versions of iPadOS 27, watchOS 27 and visionOS 27 are starting to hit Apple devices too.
You'll no longer have to install a beta of one of Apple's latest operating systems to try out Siri AI. The company has released the public versions of iOS 27, macOS 27 (aka macOS Golden Gate), iPadOS 27, watchOS 27 and visionOS 27.
As you may have deduced, the major new feature across the ecosystem is Siri AI, the long-delayed revamp of Apple's virtual assistant. Siri AI can pull your personal information from various apps and use what's on screen to bring more context to its responses. There's a new Siri app too, and the company notes usage limits may apply.
At first, Siri AI will only be available on supported devices that are set to English. Apple will add support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish next month.
Siri AI — and features that rely on it across iOS, iPadOS and watchOS — will not be available in the European Union at the outset. Apple says it's "working hard to find a path forward that preserves its users' privacy and security." The overhauled AI assistant is also on hold in China, where Apple says it's navigating regulatory requirements.
Beyond Siri AI, Apple is tweaking the Liquid Glass design language to make it more customizable and readable. The company says the new operating systems feature performance improvements that, among other things, make app launches up to 30 percent faster. Along with other iOS 27 updates, there are new AI photo editing options, support for custom EQ on AirPods, a bill-splitting feature in the US, expanded parental controls and a way to use the same phone number across two iPhones.
As always, you might not be able to install the latest operating systems immediately. There are a lot of Apple devices out in the world, and the company's servers have to handle many folks trying to update their hardware at around the same time.

title_en: With iOS 27, I’m actually using Siri again
title_fa: With iOS 27, I’m actually using Siri again
excerpt_en: Apple’s long-delayed Siri overhaul is finally here with iOS 27, and it changes how useful the assistant feels day to day.
excerpt_fa: Apple’s long-delayed Siri overhaul is finally here with iOS 27, and it changes how useful the assistant feels day to day.
content_en:
For years, I barely used Siri for anything beyond menial tasks like setting timers or alarms. That has changed with iOS 27, as I now repeatedly use Siri for complex requests and to make sense of on-screen context.
While Siri is clearly front and center in this software update by Apple, I also enjoy many of the other quality-of-life updates.
Siri
I have been using iOS 27 on my main device since the public beta version was released, and on another device through the developer beta before that. I have really enjoyed using the new Siri, often trying to find new use cases for it — and that’s possibly the biggest win for Apple, given that I, like many people, had given up on Siri before this update.
Over two years ago, Apple introduced Apple Intelligence and teased an advanced version of Siri. And after multiple delays, the company is finally shipping it, and it doesn’t disappoint. Built on the back of Google’s Gemini models, Siri is much smarter than its previous version, which was built on extended knowledge and a shaky ChatGPT integration. It also has a new logo and transition animation.
For starters, I asked Siri about several different things in the area of sports, ranging from World Cup matches to team lineups and scores. There were some hiccups in the earlier developer versions, but most of the information was correct. Siri can also take complex, multistep directions. For instance, I asked it to find small or hidden and useful features for iOS 27 and add them to a note, and it did a good job of that.
Plus, Siri can draft a message for you and send it to someone.
And because Siri can fetch context from your files, messages, and email, you can also ask it to look up a conversation, like one related to a delivery, and have it create a message for returns.
Siri’s on-screen context was a big blessing, too. I could ask trivial questions like who was the oldest player on the pitch when I was looking at lineups for two teams in the World Cup, or have it read the text on-screen out loud when I didn’t want to read. When I was on a startup’s website, I could ask Siri to look up its funding information and competitors.
One of my favorite use cases was surfing around coffee Reddit for new roasters and beans, and asking Siri to add it to a specific note. I did face a few difficulties in getting Siri to add it to the right note, but eventually I dumbed down the note’s name for better consistency.
The Camera app also now has Siri access, which means you can ask questions about things that are visible in your viewfinder. When I was at a restaurant, I asked Siri what drink I was holding. Because of the color of the drink, it said, “This is green juice,” which is a good first visual assumption. When I specified that I was at an Indian restaurant, it correctly said this could be Jaljeera or Aam Panna. (It was the latter.) I also took a photo of the restaurant’s sign and asked Siri to suggest the best items from its menu.
You can also take a photo of a coffee bag and ask Siri for the best way to brew the coffee.
With iOS 27, Siri AI gets a dedicated app that lets you return to your previous chats. In Settings, users can change Siri’s voice and expressiveness, as well.
The new assistant is positioned to work with other, third-party apps, and as developers update their apps after the operating system rolls out, it will be interesting to see if there is a smooth handoff between Siri and apps.
Apple Intelligence
Apple Intelligence powers a number of AI features in iOS 27.
For instance, Apple has sprinkled vibe-coding features within the new OS. The first is a Shortcuts creation feature that lets you describe shortcuts and automations in natural language to create them. That means you can start with a simple request, like “Show me today’s to-do items every morning at 8 a.m.” or “convert photo to JPEG,” instead of having to figure out how to craft the shortcut yourself. After the shortcut is created, you can make it more complex by adding more steps, like “convert selected photos to JPEG and share them through AirDrop.”
I always wanted to create a list of songs that I heard and liked in bars and cafes, so I made a shortcut to Shazam the song and save both the track and location.
You can also now create a custom alert in Safari to track changes to a page like a blog, item pricing, or a privacy policy page.
The Photos app has some new handy tools like “reframe” and “extend.” I found they don’t always work that well, but in some cases, they can make an image look better. Meanwhile, Apple has definitely improved its eraser functionality, which now leaves fewer strange artifacts when you remove an object.
With Apple Intelligence, when you get certain messages such as information for an event or location, smart suggestions will ask if you’d like to add them to your Calendar or Notes. What’s more, the Passwords app can now automatically change passwords on your behalf by logging into a site.
Other quality-of-life improvements
Before discussing any other features, I have to say that I love the new clipboard feature. This lets you paste anything — including links, photos, videos, and text — from one app to another easily. Once the item is in your clipboard, you see a shortcut button saying “paste from Safari” (or similar) on the keyboard, which lets you paste the item. I have been using this feature frequently, and I can’t stress enough how life-changing this is despite it being a small change.
In addition, iOS 27 addresses people’s gripes about the look of Liquid Glass. Users can now change its transparency based on their preferences. The control is granular, so you don’t have to choose from presets, either.
Apple also introduced intelligent network switching in this update, which automatically flips the connection from Wi-Fi to mobile data if there are issues with the wireless connection. The switching is seamless and very handy when you are doing important work, so you don’t lose your internet connection.

title_en: macOS 27: new Siri takes on AI productivity apps
title_fa: macOS 27: new Siri takes on AI productivity apps
excerpt_en: The two most noticeable things about macOS 27 Golden Gate are the newly updated Siri AI and the design changes that make windows and icons more consistent.
excerpt_fa: The two most noticeable things about macOS 27 Golden Gate are the newly updated Siri AI and the design changes that make windows and icons more consistent.
content_en:
The two most noticeable things about macOS 27 Golden Gate are the newly updated Siri AI and the design changes that make windows and icons more consistent. Siri AI offers the same features and capabilities as on iOS 27, but the Mac gives it access to different context — and new ways to be useful.
Over the last few years, apps and browsers have tried to learn more about your work and what you want to use AI assistants for, so they can better answer your questions or perform tasks. Today, many top web browsers, excluding Safari, come with a sidebar-based AI assistant that can look at one or multiple open tabs to provide contextual answers. Apps like Highlight, Caddy, and Littlebird can also look at your current window, then use that information as context for your queries.
The new Siri is similar. You can invoke Siri anywhere on your screen, allowing it to answer questions about what it sees, summarize information, or provide you with more details. For instance, if you are looking at an item you want to purchase, you could ask Siri to show you alternative options too.
Instead of having Siri look at the whole page, you can also select a part of the page via Apple’s new Visual Intelligence features. If you press Command + Shift + Space, you can add the currently focused window to your context for the AI.
To select a specific part, press Command + Shift + 6 to bring up a crosshair selection tool. After this, you can directly ask a question or perform an image search. Based on your selection, you will also get shortcuts like “Select,” “Add to Contact,” and “Look up Location.”
Apple has also improved Spotlight Search on Mac. You can directly ask Siri questions within Spotlight to get answers from the web, and now you can also select Applications, Files, Actions, and Clipboard to search within that particular area of context. Plus, Spotlight now allows you to run Shortcuts or look up your recent search history.
Since Siri has access to your files, emails, and messages, you can search for a variety of things that you couldn’t before. In tests, I pulled up membership IDs without opening my files, asked for details about an upcoming trip, and looked up the embargo date for an upcoming news story in the works. While I don’t find Spotlight as advanced as the highly extensible Mac productivity tool Raycast, it’s still much better than before.
Siri can also now help you with reviewing documents or performing writing tasks. Since the desktop is one of the better surfaces for writing long text, I found it to be more useful here than on the iPhone. You can do things like select a block of text and ask Siri to proofread it, improve it, or rewrite it. You can also ask Siri to draft something for you within any text box.
Safari, meanwhile, has added AI-powered page tracking, which is useful for keeping an eye on things like price drops, privacy policy changes, or new blog posts on pages when there is no RSS support. Plus, Safari can automatically organize tabs based on topics, which is handy.
One small but neat new feature is that when you download a file or rename it, the system suggests a name based on context in the Finder or when you’re saving the document.
Apart from Siri, macOS 27 Golden Gate brings design changes with new Liquid Glass icons, an adjustable slider for the Liquid Glass design, and a better way to “diffuse” content when you move windows around.
The company said that app windows have a more consistent corner radius. Sidebars now stretch edge to edge and have new colorful icons. The new operating system update also better highlights active windows.
The OS update additionally adds features like enhanced child safety controls, shared cross-platform photo albums, and an updated eraser, better search in email, app resizing for iPhone mirroring, and quick suggestions for adding events to the calendar.
Starting today, macOS 27 Golden Gate is available for MacBook Air and MacBook Pro 2020 versions with Apple Silicon or later, iMac with Apple Silicon (2021 or later), Mac Mini (2020 or later), Mac Studio (2022 or later), Mac Pro (2023 or later), and MacBook Neo. Go to System Settings > General > Software Update to get the latest version.

title_en: Fashion app Daydream uses Apple Intelligence to help you shop the outfits in your camera roll
title_fa: Fashion app Daydream uses Apple Intelligence to help you shop the outfits in your camera roll
excerpt_en: Thanks to the launch of iOS 27, Daydream's app now includes features that can turn saved outfit photos into shoppable results and search for products through Siri without opening the app.
excerpt_fa: Thanks to the launch of iOS 27, Daydream's app now includes features that can turn saved outfit photos into shoppable results and search for products through Siri without opening the app.
content_en:
Daydream, an AI-powered fashion discovery app, launched two new features on Monday to let iPhone users turn saved outfit photos into shoppable results and search for clothing and accessories through Siri, without opening the app.
The new features were built using Apple’s iOS 27 developer tools, which officially rolled out today. To use either feature, you’ll need an iPhone running iOS 27 with Siri AI enabled, along with the Daydream app installed. The app is free to download on iOS devices.
The first feature uses Apple’s image-context capabilities, letting users shop from images already saved in their Photos app. Daydream analyzes the outfit in the image, identifies its individual pieces, and automatically surfaces shoppable matches and similar styles from Daydream’s catalog of roughly 3 million products.
That means a screenshot of an outfit found on Instagram or Pinterest could become the starting point for a shopping search. Daydream can break down the image into relevant items, such as a sweater, pants, shoes, or accessories, and match them with products available through its collection. If the exact item in the photo is still available, Daydream can match the image back to the retailer selling it. If it’s no longer available, the app will instead surface similar options.
It can also handle requests for variations on what appears in an image. “I like this sweater but want it in red,” for example, is the kind of request Daydream can understand, Julie Bornstein, co-founder and CEO of Daydream, explained to TechCrunch.
The second feature is a Siri-powered natural-language search function. Users can make requests by voice or text through Siri without having to open Daydream’s app.
A user could say, “Hey, Siri, search Daydream for a cool blazer for my board meeting on Monday,” and Daydream then provides results personalized to them.
Bornstein adds that the experience can be more tailored if users have set up Daydream’s “Style Passport,” which asks for details such as their sizes, preferred brands, personal style, and budget.
The company joins a growing number of AI shopping tools designed to rethink product discovery, such as big names like Google and Amazon, as well as some smaller players like Onton and Alta. But Bornstein believes that Daydream’s latest features offer something special that a lot of these other tools just can’t match.
“Most visual search tools don’t have the fashion category expertise, so they return results that don’t feel accurate, from brands that aren’t credible, or they link you to nonshoppable images,” she said.
The launch fits into Daydream’s broader bet on AI-powered fashion shopping. The company sees these new features as more than stand-alone shopping tools. Its longer-term ambition is to build a shopping agent.
“This is one step toward the bigger vision, [which is] a shopping agent that understands someone’s style well enough to work across every surface in their life, not just on one surface,” Bornstein said. “Expect us to keep going deeper into on-device intelligence and further into the everyday moments where people are already discovering things they want.”
Daydream’s app launched last year and touts that it has more than 1.5 million shoppers browsing products from more than 325 retailers and 10,000 brands. Its retail lineup includes brands such as Anthropologie, Dolce & Gabbana, Uniqlo, J.Crew, Reformation, Gucci, and Nordstrom.

title_en: Valve Steam Frame review: Solid standalone VR that's too little, too late
title_fa: Valve Steam Frame review: Solid standalone VR that's too little, too late
excerpt_en: The Steam Frame is a pretty great standalone VR headset, it's just too bad it costs over $1,000.
excerpt_fa: The Steam Frame is a pretty great standalone VR headset, it's just too bad it costs over $1,000.
content_en:
Valve Steam Frame review: Solid standalone VR that's too little, too late
A $1,059 VR headset today is just madness.
Much like the Steam Machine, Valve's Steam Frame VR headset feels like a device that should have shipped five years ago. As a standalone wireless headset, it's directly competing with Meta's Quest lineup, even though that company has seriously scaled back its VR ambitions. The ability to play many Steam VR games right within the Steam Frame would have been cool several years ago, but in 2026 there aren't many developers left building ambitious new virtual reality experiences. Oh yeah, the Steam Frame also starts at a whopping $1,059 with just 256GB of storage, a far cry from the heyday of the $200 Quest 2, or even the current $600 Quest 3. Just who the hell is this VR headset really for?
The cynic in me thinks the Steam Frame is a sign of just how out of touch Valve is with the broader VR industry. Perhaps the company planned to release something closer to the Quest 3's launch in 2023, back when VR seemed like an escape from the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic. In today's chaotic economy, I can't imagine anyone being excited to shell out over $1,000 for the Steam Frame just to jump into the same VR games they've been playing for a decade. And while there are a handful of new VR releases today, it's far from a thriving category of games.
After testing the Steam Frame for the past week, I can't deny it does some things well. It delivers an expansive and sharp VR experience without the need for any cables. It's also nice to play 2D games on a gigantic virtual screen, and you can also stream over more demanding VR and 2D titles from your gaming PC. But it's not something I can recommend at its current price, not when the Quest 3S and Quest 3 can deliver similar VR experiences for $350 and $600, respectively.
What's notable about the Steam Frame?
The Steam Frame looks like a far slimmer version of the Valve Index, the company's first stab at premium VR hardware. The front display area is much shorter, there's no clunky plastic bar connecting the front and rear portions of the headset, and it weighs just under a pound (440 grams). That makes it slightly lighter than the 1.13-pound (515 grams) Quest 3. A large cushion surrounds the removable face gasket, and it's also buoyed by additional cushioning along the rear battery.
Despite being much lighter than a typical headset, though, the Steam Frame still looks unapologetically like older VR hardware. It's practically archaic compared to the leaked images of Meta's next-gen "Project Phoenix" headset, which looks like a sleek pair of large sunglasses. Valve clearly isn't going for much mainstream appeal here — it's catering to the gamers who just want a standalone headset for Steam VR.
The Steam Frame's two large LCD pancake lenses deliver 2,160 by 2,160 pixels per eye, and they offer between a 72Hz and 144Hz refresh rate. Valve says the latter figure is currently experimental, and since it's also forcing the device to do more work, you can also expect it to be far more battery-demanding. For the price, it would have been nice to see Valve bump up to micro-OLED displays, like the Apple Vision Pro and Bigscreen Beyond. The Steam Frame also features eye-tracking sensors for foveated rendering, which lets it instantly show you the sharpest VR picture wherever your eyes are looking.
Under the hood, the Steam Frame is powered by a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 CPU, an eight-core chip that should be significantly faster than the six-core Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 in the Quest 3. It also features 16GB of RAM and comes with either 256GB or 1TB of Universal Flash Storage (UFS). And, thankfully, there's a microSD card slot for adding more storage.
The Steam Frame itself doesn't have a ton of onboard controls. There are volume buttons along the left side, as well as power and auxiliary buttons along the right. A small expansion port on the bottom also lets you connect accessories like Arcturus's RGB camera. (Unfortunately, its internal cameras are monochrome.)
Notably, the Steam Frame also ships with a wireless PC dongle for direct 6GHz Wi-Fi 6e streaming. While the Quest headsets also let you stream games wireless from your gaming PC, they used your existing Wi-Fi network to do so, which often led to unreliable connections. Valve says its dongle can also work together with your Wi-Fi network to ensure a smoother streaming experience. (You could also connect Quest headsets to PCs with USB 3.0 cables, which avoids wireless interference issues, but loses cord-free convenience.)
Valve's new Steam Frame controllers are practically copies of the designs from Oculus (before Meta's acquisition) and other VR headset makers. They both have two analog sticks, two system buttons, analog triggers and grip buttons. As usual, the left controller has a traditional directional pad, while the right has four face buttons. Valve's unique Index controllers, which were gripped tightly to your hands at all times, are no more. Still, you can replicate that functionality with the Frame's $59 Ergonomic Accessories Kit, which has hand straps and an additional top head strap. It's not too surprising to see Valve fall in line with the standard VR gamepad setup, as it will ultimately make life easier for consumers and developers alike.
Set up for disappointment
I'll admit, the first emotion I felt after setting up the Steam Frame was a deep sense of disappointment. It's 2026, and once again I'm staring at the same library of Steam VR titles I've had for the past decade. Nobody is going to shell out $1,059 just to play Beat Saber again. And aside from a new version of Half-Life Alyx that's rebuilt to run standalone on the Steam Frame, Valve isn't releasing any major new VR titles to celebrate the headset's launch.
While there are Steam VR titles being released regularly by indie studios, there hasn't been anything that's truly excited me since Alyx was released in 2020, hence my...

title_en: Microsoft’s new AI ‘code of conduct’ tells models not to hack systems or trick humans
title_fa: Microsoft’s new AI ‘code of conduct’ tells models not to hack systems or trick humans
excerpt_en: The code of conduct lays out general principles that Microsoft AI models should uphold — supporting humans rather than replacing them, for instance, and accelerating human flourishing — as well as specific safety constraints meant to implement those principles.
excerpt_fa: The code of conduct lays out general principles that Microsoft AI models should uphold — supporting humans rather than replacing them, for instance, and accelerating human flourishing — as well as specific safety constraints meant to implement those principles.
content_en:
As the AI world shifts its focus to safety and alignment, Microsoft has released a new AI code of conduct meant to guide AI models away from dangerous behavior.
The document is more low level than Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s recent call for pacing the frontier, instead focusing on the values and red lines that guide model training within Microsoft AI. Still, the result is a comprehensive guide as to how Microsoft approaches AI safety and how those ideas are implemented in practice.
The document begins with the prediction that, in the next decade, superintelligent AI systems will surpass human performance in most tasks. “Containing, controlling, and aligning such a powerful force is one of the greatest challenges humanity has ever faced,” the code of conduct states. “We must therefore be completely clear about why we are inventing these systems and how we intend to control them.”
The code of conduct also lays out general principles that Microsoft AI models should uphold — supporting humans rather than replacing them, for instance, and accelerating human flourishing — as well as specific safety constraints meant to implement those principles.
Under Microsoft’s system, each model has an overarching code of conduct that overrides the preferences of individual users or any specific tasks. That includes “absolute constraints” forbidding cyberattacks, nuclear weapons, or deepfake production. It also includes broader provisions against a general loss of human control.
“MAI Models will not use adaptive, deceptive, self-reinforcing, collusion, or other mechanisms to evade or defeat human oversight so that they can no longer be reliably directed, modified, or shut down by authorized people or systems,” the document reads.
The release comes amid an unprecedented focus on AI safety, driven by a string of rogue-agent incidents, as well as the abrupt resignation of an Anthropic employee, who cited the growing risk that AI would cause human extinction.
Together with Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI, Microsoft has broadly embraced a general approach of pacing the frontier, with particular support for embedded evaluators in AI labs.
“We welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote online. “We also welcome ideas like ’embedded evaluators’ and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk.”

title_en: Waymo opens robotaxi service in Las Vegas
title_fa: Waymo opens robotaxi service in Las Vegas
excerpt_en: Las Vegas will be Waymo's 15th commercial robotaxi market.
excerpt_fa: Las Vegas will be Waymo's 15th commercial robotaxi market.
content_en:
Waymo has begun to open up its robotaxi service to the public in Las Vegas, just a few weeks after receiving final approval from Nevada transportation regulators.
The Alphabet-owned company said Monday it will invite public riders on a rolling basis, following a robotaxi launch playbook it has followed in 14 other cities.
Waymo is starting with “dozens” of its new Ojai minivan robotaxis, which will serve an area of Las Vegas that includes the Strip south of Highway 589 and into Boulder Junction, according to a spokesperson. Waymo’s fleet and service area will eventually scale. For now, members of the public will have to request an invite and hope to receive an access code. Typically, Waymo opens the service up to everyone within a month or two of its official launch.
The announcement follows a busy few weeks for Waymo as it tries to ramp up its operations across the United States and Europe as Tesla, Zoox, and other competitors attempt to close on its lead. Earlier this month, the company began offering its robotaxis to invited members of the public in Denver, San Diego, and Tampa.
Las Vegas, where competitors Tesla and Motional are also planning to launch commercial robotaxi services, is Waymo’s 15th market. Zoox is already operating a commercial service in Las Vegas. Waymo also operates in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, Phoenix, and the San Francisco Bay Area. The company launched, and then paused, service in San Antonio.
Waymo’s entry into Las Vegas follows approval by the Nevada Transportation Authority to operate commercial robotaxi services in Clark County, home to Las Vegas. Tesla and Uber also received approval from the agency.
Waymo has been authorized to operate up to 1,000 autonomous vehicles over the next year, Tesla is allowed to deploy up to 5,000, and Uber is allowed up to 1,000 robotaxis, which it will operate through partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox. Together, these permits would deploy up to 7,000 robotaxis across the county over the next 12 months.
It’s unlikely that the three companies will reach those numbers. Today, Waymo has a fleet of more than 4,000 robotaxis, which are spread across more than a dozen cities. During a meeting in August, Tesla’s Cybercab chief engineer Eric Early told state regulators that the company would be “extremely happy and satisfied if we could get ourselves up to 2,500, maybe a bit higher than that in the next year.”
Even without reaching those figures, the city could be saturated with robotaxis in the next year.
Update: This article was updated to clarify that Zoox is already operating a commercial robotaxi service in Las Vegas.

title_en: Sources say Automattic’s board is out after failed attempt to oust CEO Matt Mullenweg
title_fa: Sources say Automattic’s board is out after failed attempt to oust CEO Matt Mullenweg
excerpt_en: Given that these departed board members were those who voted to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence to begin with, it makes sense that a board shakeup has taken place.
excerpt_fa: Given that these departed board members were those who voted to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence to begin with, it makes sense that a board shakeup has taken place.
content_en:
Automattic’s board is out, multiple sources have confirmed to TechCrunch, after last week’s attempt to oust CEO Matt Mullenweg by voting to put him on a paid leave of absence.
After the vote, Mullenweg, the WordPress founder and CEO of WordPress.com parent company Automattic, accused the board of conspiring against him in a post on Automattic’s Slack. On Friday, TechCrunch exclusively reported that Mullenweg told the company’s staff that he was back in control of the company, also via Slack post. Automattic confirmed to TechCrunch on Saturday that he had returned.
Initially, we heard from sources that Toni Schneider, a founding CEO at Automattic who now leads the open social network Bluesky, had resigned his Automattic board seat. Schneider has since removed a paragraph from his bio page on his personal website that had noted his contributions at Automattic.
Previously, Schneider’s website read: “I also contribute actively at Automattic, the open source company behind WordPress.com and WooCommerce. I was Automattic’s founding CEO and continue to support internal projects and investments as a board member and special advisor.”
We’ve also heard that Mullenweg removed the two other board members, Sue Decker and Gen. Ann Dunwoody. (We later confirmed that Mullenweg removed Dunwoody, but Decker resigned).
Decker’s LinkedIn bio has been updated to confirm that she served on Automattic’s board from March 2020 through September 2026, despite her name still appearing on Automattic’s Board of Directors page at the time of publication.
When asked by TechCrunch about the board changes, Automattic declined to provide specifics, but offered a statement acknowledging that people have left.
Via an email that arrived after midnight PT on Sunday, an Automattic spokesperson shared the following:
“Matt and Automattic’s leadership team have great respect for everyone involved. While we can’t comment on specific individuals, we’re thankful for their contributions to Automattic and its mission, and we remain excited about what’s ahead with Matt at the helm. Matt was away for only 33 hours and 20 minutes—we’re now back to work,” the spokesperson said.
Given that these departed board members were those who voted to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence to begin with, it makes sense that a board shakeup has taken place. It also explains how Mullenweg’s return to his position as CEO would have the “full support of the board,” as a statement issued on Saturday indicated.
TechCrunch is hearing from sources that Automattic may make an internal announcement about the new board sometime on Monday.
In addition to the board departures, Automattic’s Chief Legal Officer Andy Missan also updated his LinkedIn bio, showing he’s no longer at the company as of September 2026. We understand Mullenweg let him go, along with CFO Mark Davies, who was to be the interim CEO.
What prompted the board’s vote still remains unclear. Mullenweg and Automattic are involved in a high-profile lawsuit with a WordPress hosting company, WP Engine. Mullenweg has accused the company of infringing on the WordPress trademark and not sufficiently contributing in terms of engineering hours or money to the open source WordPress effort. Earlier this year, WP Engine claimed in a court filing that Automattic planned to target other competitors with royalty fees.
More recently, it has accused Mullenweg of allegedly destroying evidence related to the case in apps like WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram. Last year, Mullenweg had deactivated the accounts of several WordPress contributors over alleged plans to fork the open source software.
Updated after initial publication with additional information about the departures.
Do you have more information? You can reach Sarah Perez at sarahp@techcrunch.com or @sarahperez.01 on Signal.

title_en: Only at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: What happens when OpenAI ships your roadmap?
title_fa: Only at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: What happens when OpenAI ships your roadmap?
excerpt_en: If you're building an AI company, the question isn't whether foundation models will continue to evolve. It's whether your company will continue creating value as they do. Don't miss this interactive session on the Builders Stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.
excerpt_fa: If you're building an AI company, the question isn't whether foundation models will continue to evolve. It's whether your company will continue creating value as they do. Don't miss this interactive session on the Builders Stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.
content_en:
For AI founders, the biggest competitive threat may no longer be another startup. It may be the platform you’re building on. Every major release from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google raises the same question: What happens if the feature you’ve spent the last year building suddenly becomes part of the platform?
It’s a question reshaping product strategy, fundraising, and company valuations across the AI ecosystem. Not long ago, founders worried about competing with other startups. Today, they’re competing with foundation model companies introducing entirely new capabilities every few months.
That changes almost every strategic decision — from what products to build and where to differentiate to how to raise capital and create lasting value. The conversation moves from “Can we build it?” to “Can we still own it?”
That’s the challenge at the heart of “What Happens When OpenAI Ships Your Roadmap,” a Builders Stage session featuring leaders Michel Tricot (Airbyte), Rob Toews (Radical Ventures), and Linda Tong (Webflow), at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, taking place October 13–15 at Moscone West in San Francisco. Disrupt is the flagship startup event where 10,000+ founders, investors, and operators gather for 250+ sessions exploring the market forces reshaping how startups are built, funded, and scaled.
See how founders are responding to AI’s biggest competitive shift. Secure your pass to Disrupt with savings of up to $200 before rates increase on September 25.
When products become features
One of the biggest strategic risks facing AI startups today isn’t losing to another founder — it’s discovering that your competitive advantage has become someone else’s product update.
That’s the reality this session is designed to confront. As foundation models rapidly evolve, capabilities that once differentiated an AI startup can quickly become table stakes. Increasingly, founders aren’t just competing with other startups — they’re competing with the platforms powering the AI ecosystem itself.
Here, founders will examine why the next generation of AI winners may not be defined by the smartest models. They’ll be defined by everything the models can’t easily replace: proprietary data, deeply embedded workflows, customer relationships, domain expertise, and trust.
The reality founders increasingly need to prepare for is, “Can we build something customers will still value after the next model release?”
This session explores where defensibility still exists, how founders can respond when AI giants move into adjacent markets, and what separates companies that become features from those that remain businesses.
Learn how founders are building beyond the next model release. Register for Disrupt today and save up to $200.
Three perspectives on AI’s biggest strategic question, all laid out on the Builders Stage
To unpack this challenge, the Builders Stage session brings together a founder, an operator, and an investor, each offering a different view on creating defensible AI companies.
How do you create lasting value when the technology underneath your product keeps changing?
Michel Tricot has spent his career building the data integration infrastructure that powers analytics, operations, and AI. As CEO and co-founder of Airbyte, he has grown the open source platform to more than 7,000 customers — including 18% of the Fortune 500 — giving him firsthand insight into where durable businesses are built beyond the foundation model.
How do software companies stay differentiated as AI reshapes customer expectations?
As CEO of Webflow, Linda Tong is leading one of the industry’s top visual development platforms through one of SaaS’s biggest technology shifts. Her experience scaling Webflow and leading teams at Google, Cisco, and the NFL gives founders practical insight into evolving products without losing competitive advantage.
What convinces investors that an AI company will still matter three years from now?
At Radical Ventures, partner Rob Toews evaluates AI startups every day, identifying where competitive advantages still exist — and where products risk becoming features.
Together, they bring unique perspectives to one defining question facing AI startups today: What can you build that the platforms can’t simply ship themselves?
Secure your Disrupt pass and hear how founders are building companies, not just AI features.
Learn how to build lasting AI defensibility at Disrupt

title_en: Superhuman acquires YC-backed notetaker Fathom as productivity platforms push for agentic work
title_fa: Superhuman acquires YC-backed notetaker Fathom as productivity platforms push for agentic work
excerpt_en: The notetaker offers a generous free plan, and that has resulted in over 400,000 monthly active users. The company said that over 1 million people have recorded meetings until now.
excerpt_fa: The notetaker offers a generous free plan, and that has resulted in over 400,000 monthly active users. The company said that over 1 million people have recorded meetings until now.
content_en:
Superhuman is joining the cadre of productivity platforms launching notetakers — but rather than building one internally, it is acquiring Y Combinator-backed Fathom.
AI-powered productivity platforms aim to automate work. Typically, that automation is triggered when a user types prompts and creates workflows. It would be even better, however, if AI could proactively start work, and for that, the topics and action items discussed in meetings are key. Hence the desire by Superhuman and similar platforms to move into notetaking.
To date, Fathom, which was founded in 2020, has raised over $30 million in funding, and it was valued at $94 million in 2024, according to data from PitchBook. Its investors include Zoom Apps Fund, Telescope Partners, BoxOne Ventures, Character Capital, and Maven Ventures. Its cap table also includes individuals such as Reddit CEO Steve Huffman, former Twitch CEO Emmett Shear, and Cruise co-founder Kyle Vogt.
The notetaker offers a generous free plan, and that has resulted in over 400,000 monthly active users. The company said that over 1 million people have recorded meetings until now.
TechCrunch learned that earlier this year, Superhuman tested a notetaker internally with select users, but eventually chose to acquire a finished product to integrate with its productivity suite, with AI at the center. Shishir Mehrotra, Superhuman’s CEO, acknowledged this; he said that in the process of testing, the company realized how hard it is to create a notetaker.
“We’ve been working internally on this area for a while as well. I think it greatly increased our confidence in the demand in this category. It also becomes very clear how deep the products in this category are and how much you need to build. A lot of these products make the job feel really easy, but it’s actually quite tricky to do a great job in all parts [of meeting recording],” Mehrotra told TechCrunch over a call.
Mehrotra said that he was impressed with some of the technical intricacies built by the Fathom team, but didn’t elaborate on which ones. He did tease that with a notetaker, Superhuman can work on surfacing meeting context in real time.
Competition in the meeting notetaker space is intense, and startups like Granola, Read AI, and new entrant Wispr have raised millions of dollars to aid that growth. Despite having a healthy customer base or revenue run rate, venture-backed notetakers are feeling the heat from the market to do more than just notetaking. Some of these factors did matter in Superhuman acquiring Fathom, while Fathom’s CEO Richard White said that Superhuman’s 40 million user base was a good opportunity to reach users at scale.
“The reach of Superhuman is massive. I have always thought about M&A in terms of speed of building a product that everyone uses, and a part of that comes down to distribution. If we were to operate Fathom as a stand-alone company, we would have to build a lot of things that are already in the Superhuman platform,” he said.
On the platform front, Superhuman already has an email client, a docs app, a calendar, a database solution, and a newly launched AI agent builder platform. With a meeting notetaker in the middle, Superhuman can draft emails, update data entries, schedule follow-up meetings, and have AI agents start work and extract insights from meeting data.

title_en: Hear how AI can engineer nature’s comeback at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
title_fa: Hear how AI can engineer nature’s comeback at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
excerpt_en: Not long ago, bringing an extinct species back to life belonged to science fiction. Today, it's the mission of a billion-dollar startup. Join the conversation with one of tech's most unconventional founders. Secure your Disrupt pass today.
excerpt_fa: Not long ago, bringing an extinct species back to life belonged to science fiction. Today, it's the mission of a billion-dollar startup. Join the conversation with one of tech's most unconventional founders. Secure your Disrupt pass today.
content_en:
Not long ago, bringing an extinct species back to life belonged to science fiction. Today, it’s the mission of a billion-dollar startup. Advances in artificial intelligence, genetics, and computational biology are changing what’s possible in conservation research, raising questions that extend far beyond the laboratory. If technology can help revive extinct species, should it? And what role should AI play in shaping the future of biodiversity?
Those are the questions at the center of “Can We Engineer Nature’s Comeback?,” a Real World AI Stage fireside chat at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.
Joining the conversation is Ben Lamm, co-founder and CEO of Colossal Biosciences, a company pioneering efforts to bring extinct species back through advances in synthetic biology and AI. Rather than focusing solely on the science, the discussion explores the technologies behind de-extinction, the role AI now plays in modern biology, and the growing debate over whether engineering nature represents a conservation breakthrough — or a distraction from protecting the ecosystems we already have.
Disrupt returns to Moscone West in San Francisco, October 13–15, bringing together 10,000+ founders, investors, and operators for 250+ sessions exploring the technologies and market forces shaping what’s next. Hear one of this year’s most provocative conversations. Secure your pass to Disrupt.
Where AI meets biology
AI is already reshaping software, robotics, and scientific research. Biology may be its next frontier. Researchers are using AI to analyze genetic data, model biological systems, and accelerate discovery. Companies like Colossal are pushing those advances even further, applying AI alongside synthetic biology to questions that until recently belonged in science fiction.
This session explores where those technologies intersect and what happens when AI moves beyond digital systems and into the natural world. For founders working at the intersection of deep tech, life sciences, and AI, it’s an opportunity to hear how one of the industry’s most ambitious companies is approaching problems few organizations have attempted to solve.
Explore the Real World AI Stage lineup and register for Disrupt today.
A founder building at the edge of what’s possible
Ben Lamm has spent more than two decades building companies at the intersection of AI and emerging technologies. A serial entrepreneur, he’s built businesses focused on solving complex challenges — from enterprise AI and critical infrastructure to conversational intelligence. Before founding Colossal Biosciences, he launched several pioneering technology companies, including Hypergiant, Conversable, and Chaotic Moon, which were later acquired by Trive Capital, LivePerson, and Accenture, respectively.
Today, he’s applying that entrepreneurial mindset to an entirely different challenge: using AI and synthetic biology to explore de-extinction as a conservation tool. That work has made Colossal one of the most closely watched — and most debated — companies in science and technology. As CEO, Lamm sits at the center of conversations about biodiversity, climate resilience, emerging technologies, and the responsibilities that come with engineering living systems.
His experience offers founders a rare look at what happens when breakthrough technology doesn’t just disrupt an industry, challenging how we think about what’s possible.
Join the conversation with one of tech’s most unconventional founders. Secure your Disrupt pass today.
A conversation bigger than de-extinction, only at Disrupt 2026
Reviving extinct species captures headlines. The broader questions may prove even more significant. As AI becomes part of scientific discovery, conversations about technology increasingly extend beyond software into medicine, biology, conservation, and climate science. Those advances bring new possibilities, but they also raise difficult questions about how, and where, these tools should be used.
Whether you view de-extinction as a scientific breakthrough, a conservation strategy, or a controversial experiment, the discussion reaches far beyond any single species. It asks what role emerging technologies should play in solving some of the world’s most complex problems and who gets to decide.
Lock in your pass to Disrupt with up to $200 in savings, and join the conversation about where AI, biology, and innovation intersect.
